The fit summary table consolidates all model comparison evidence in one place. Each row represents a model; green-highlighted rows are the preferred NB models.
R² for NB Office ≈ 1 − (23,430 / 29,459) ≈ 0.205: this is considered excellent for individual-level health survey data. The threshold of 0.20 is the conventional benchmark for a 'good model' in social and health sciences. The ER model (R² ≈ 0.156) is good — ER visits are harder to predict because they include both necessary emergencies and avoidable ones driven by lack of primary care access.


## Hidden Exclusion Analysis

```{r nb_hidden_exclusion}
hidden_df <- meps_adults %>%
  group_by(any_barrier, any_chronic) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_office = round(mean(office_visits, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    avg_er     = round(mean(er_visits, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    n          = n(),
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Group = case_when(
      any_barrier == 0 & any_chronic == 0 ~ "No Barrier / No Chronic",
      any_barrier == 0 & any_chronic == 1 ~ "No Barrier / Chronic",
      any_barrier == 1 & any_chronic == 0 ~ "Barrier / No Chronic",
      any_barrier == 1 & any_chronic == 1 ~ "Barrier + Chronic"
    )
  )

knitr::kable(hidden_df,
             caption = "Average Utilization: Barriers × Chronic Status",
             col.names = c("Barrier", "Chronic", "Avg Office Visits", "Avg ER Visits", "N", "Group")) %>%
  kable_styling()

hidden_df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(avg_office, avg_er),
               names_to = "type", values_to = "average") %>%
  mutate(type = ifelse(type == "avg_office", "Office Visits", "ER Visits")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Group, y = average, fill = type)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~type, scales = "free_y")+
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1", name = "") +
  labs(title = "Average Utilization by Barrier and Chronic Status",
       x = "", y = "Average Visits") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))


```

## The Hidden Exclusion Analysis 

The code groups all patients into four cells defined by two binary variables — any_barrier (has at least one access barrier) and any_chronic (has at least one chronic condition). For each cell, it computes the mean office visits and mean ER visits.

The Four Groups
 
Group	                     Barriers	       Chronic     	Avg Office (Expected)	      Avg ER (Expected)	              Role in Analysis
No Barrier / No Chronic	     No	              No	        3 – 5	                        0.10 – 0.20	        Healthy baseline — reference
No Barrier / Chronic	       No	              Yes	        7 – 12	                      0.30 – 0.50	        Need met — benchmark for chronic patients
Barrier / No Chronic	      Yes	              No	        2 – 4	                        0.20 – 0.30	        Barriers without clinical need
Barrier + Chronic	          Yes	             Yes	         5 – 9	                      0.50 – 0.90	        HIDDEN EXCLUSION: need suppressed, ER elevated


The critical contrast is between the two chronic condition groups:
•	No Barrier / Chronic: patients with chronic conditions who have access to care use it appropriately. Office visits are high; ER visits are moderate and likely reflect acute episodes within a managed care context.
•	Barrier + Chronic: patients with the same clinical profile but structural barriers. Office visits are substantially lower — not because they are healthier, but because they cannot access care. ER visits are higher — the emergency department becomes the residual access point for unmet primary care need.

The Two Circuits of American Healthcare
What we can conclude is there's an existence of two parallel care circuits in the American healthcare system:

*Circuit*	                       
Ambulatory care circuit	Insured, 
*Who Uses It*
high-income, educated
 *Driven By*
elderly	Insurance + resources to navigate system
*Outcome*
Appropriate preventive and chronic care management

*Circuit*	
Emergency care circuit	
*Who Uses It*
Uninsured, poor, Medicaid, 
*Driven By*
low education,Lack of alternatives — ER as default	
*Outcome*
Crisis-driven care, avoidable hospitalizations


These two circuits are not independent choices. The patients in the emergency care circuit are not there because they prefer it — they are there because structural barriers have closed the ambulatory care circuit to them. The regression models quantify this: the same clinical need (same n_chronic, same poor_health) leads to 4× more office visits for an insured high-income patient than for an uninsured poor one.

The American healthcare system does not distribute care according to need , it distributes care according to the structural capacity to access it. 
The uninsured are not healthier than the insured; they simply cannot afford scheduled visits. 
The poor are not receiving less total healthcare; they are receiving it in the emergency room instead of the doctor's office. 
Racial minorities face barriers that persist even after controlling for income and insurance. 
The sickest patients with access barriers do not receive less care because they need less, they receive it at the wrong time, in the wrong place, at greater cost and with worse clinical outcomes.

---

# Generalized Linear Mixed Models

Parts 2 and 3 treated both `region` and `ins_status` as fixed-effect covariates — categorical predictors with specific, estimable coefficients relative to a reference category. This is the appropriate choice when the goal is to quantify the directional effect of each level: how much does the South differ from the Northeast, or how much do the uninsured differ from the privately insured?

A Generalized Linear Mixed Model (GLMM) with either variable as a random effect asks a fundamentally different question: not how a specific group differs from the reference, but how much unexplained variability in healthcare utilization exists at the group level, beyond what individual-level predictors already capture.

## GLMM: Region as Random Effect  (Office Visits)
```{r glmm_office, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
theta_office <- model_nb_office$theta

glmm_office <- glmer(
  office_visits ~ ins_status + age_group + sex + race_eth + povcat +
    n_chronic + poor_health + educ_cat + any_barrier + (1 | region),
  family  = negative.binomial(theta = theta_office),
  data    = meps_adults,
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 1e5))
)

summary(glmm_office)
```

```{r glmm_office_results}
vc_office <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(glmm_office))
icc_office <- vc_office$vcov[1] / (vc_office$vcov[1] + (pi^2 / 3))

cat("Random-effect variance (region):", round(vc_office$vcov[1], 4), "\n")
cat("Intraclass Correlation (ICC):", round(icc_office, 4), "\n\n")


glmm_office_tidy <- broom.mixed::tidy(glmm_office, effects = "fixed",
                                       exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
                                       filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
                                      rename(IRR = estimate, CI_low = conf.low, CI_high = conf.high)

knitr::kable(
  glmm_office_tidy %>% dplyr::select(term, IRR, CI_low, CI_high, p.value),
  digits  = 3,
  caption = "Fixed-Effect IRRs — Office Visits"
) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) %>%
  row_spec(which(glmm_office_tidy$p.value < 0.05), bold = TRUE)
```

```{r glmm_office_ranef, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5, echo=FALSE}

# Caterpillar plot of region random effects
ranef_df <- as.data.frame(lme4::ranef(glmm_office, condVar = TRUE)$region) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("region") %>%
  rename(intercept = `(Intercept)`)

condvar <- attr(lme4::ranef(glmm_office, condVar = TRUE)$region, "postVar")
ranef_df$se <- sqrt(condvar[1, 1, ])

ggplot(ranef_df, aes(x = reorder(region, intercept), y = intercept)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#2C7BB6") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = intercept - 1.96 * se,
                    ymax = intercept + 1.96 * se), width = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Region Random Effects — Office Visits", subtitle = "Conditional modes ± 1.96 SE",
       x = "", y = "Random Intercept (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r glmm_office_fit, echo=FALSE}
r2_glmm <- MuMIn::r.squaredGLMM(glmm_office)
cat("Marginal R² (fixed effects only):  ", round(r2_glmm[1, "R2m"], 4), "\n")
cat("Conditional R² (fixed + random):   ", round(r2_glmm[1, "R2c"], 4), "\n")
cat("AIC NB fixed-effect model:       ", round(AIC(model_nb_office), 1), "\n")
cat("AIC GLMM (region random):        ", round(AIC(glmm_office), 1), "\n")
```

The random-effect variance for region is 0.0098, yielding an ICC of 0.003. This means that only 0.3% of the residual variability in office visit counts is attributable to between-region differences — the remaining 99.7% reflects heterogeneity among individuals within the same region. The caterpillar plot confirms this: all four regional random intercepts are close to zero, indicating that no region deviates meaningfully from the population average once individual characteristics are held constant.

The marginal R² of 0.265 rises to just 0.269 when the regional random effect is added — an increment of 0.004 that confirms geography contributes almost nothing beyond what insurance status, income, age, health status, and education already capture.

The AIC comparison reinforces this conclusion: the fixed-effect Negative Binomial model from Part 3 (AIC = 119,822) outperforms the GLMM (AIC = 119,835). The fixed-effect specification remains the preferred model for office visit counts.

The fixed-effect IRRs are virtually identical to those from Part 3, which is itself a robustness result: insurance status remains the dominant structural predictor, the income gradient is monotone and dose-responsive, and clinical need predictors retain their magnitudes. The individual-level estimates are not confounded by any unobserved regional clustering.


## GLMM: Region as Random Effect (ER Visits)
```{r glmm_er, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

theta_er <- model_nb_er$theta

glmm_er <- glmer(
  er_visits ~ ins_status + age_group + sex + race_eth + povcat +
    n_chronic + poor_health + educ_cat + any_barrier +
    (1 | region),
  family = MASS::negative.binomial(theta = theta_er),
  data = meps_adults,
  control = glmerControl(
    optimizer = "bobyqa",
    optCtrl = list(maxfun = 1e5)
  )
)

summary(glmm_er)
```

```{r glmm_er_results, echo=FALSE}
vc_er   <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(glmm_er))
icc_er  <- vc_er$vcov[1] / (vc_er$vcov[1] + (pi^2 / 3))

cat("Random-effect variance (region):", round(vc_er$vcov[1], 4), "\n")
cat("Intraclass Correlation (ICC):", round(icc_er, 4), "\n\n")

glmm_er_tidy <- broom.mixed::tidy(glmm_er, effects = "fixed",
                                   exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
                                   filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
                                  rename(IRR = estimate, CI_low = conf.low, CI_high = conf.high)

knitr::kable(
  glmm_er_tidy %>% dplyr::select(term, IRR, CI_low, CI_high, p.value),
  digits  = 3,
  caption = "Fixed-Effect IRRs — ER Visits"
) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) %>%
  row_spec(which(glmm_er_tidy$p.value < 0.05), bold = TRUE)

r2_glmm_er <- MuMIn::r.squaredGLMM(glmm_er)
cat("Marginal R²:   ", round(r2_glmm_er[1, "R2m"], 4), "\n")
cat("Conditional R²:", round(r2_glmm_er[1, "R2c"], 4), "\n")
cat("AIC NB fixed-effect model:", round(AIC(model_nb_er), 1), "\n")
cat("AIC GLMM (region random): ", round(AIC(glmm_er), 1), "\n")
```

The pattern for emergency department visits is even more conclusive. The random-effect variance for region is 0.0022, yielding an ICC of 0.0007 — effectively zero. The marginal and conditional R² are identical to three decimal places (0.074 and 0.075 respectively), and the AIC of the GLMM (23,741) is marginally worse than the fixed-effect NB model (23,739), confirming that the regional random effect adds no information for emergency utilization either.

Taken together, the two GLMM models for region deliver a consistent and substantively important message: the structural disparities in healthcare utilization documented in Parts 2 and 3 are a national phenomenon, not a regional one. The South does not produce more hidden exclusion than the Northeast because it is in the South; it does so because it concentrates more uninsured, lower-income, and higher-barrier individuals. 


## GLMM: Insurance Status as Random Effect (Office Visits)
```{r glmm_ins_office, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

theta_office <- model_nb_office$theta

glmm_ins_office <- glmer(
  office_visits ~ region + age_group + sex + race_eth + povcat +
    n_chronic + poor_health + educ_cat + any_barrier + (1 | ins_status),
  family  = negative.binomial(theta = theta_office),
  data    = meps_adults,
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 1e5))
)

summary(glmm_ins_office)
```

```{r glmm_ins_office_results, echo=FALSE}
vc_ins_office <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(glmm_ins_office))
icc_ins_office <- vc_ins_office$vcov[1] / (vc_ins_office$vcov[1] + (pi^2 / 3))

cat("Random-effect variance (insurance status):", round(vc_ins_office$vcov[1], 4), "\n")
cat("Intraclass Correlation (ICC):", round(icc_ins_office, 4), "\n\n")

glmm_ins_office_tidy <- broom.mixed::tidy(glmm_ins_office, effects = "fixed",
                                           exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
                                           filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
                                           rename(IRR = estimate, CI_low = conf.low, CI_high = conf.high)

knitr::kable(
  glmm_ins_office_tidy %>% dplyr::select(term, IRR, CI_low, CI_high, p.value),
  digits  = 3,
  caption = "GLMM: Fixed-Effect IRRs — Office Visits"
) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) %>%
  row_spec(which(glmm_ins_office_tidy$p.value < 0.05), bold = TRUE)
```

```{r glmm_ins_office_ranef, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5, echo=FALSE}
# Caterpillar plot of insurance status random effects
ranef_ins_df <- as.data.frame(lme4::ranef(glmm_ins_office, condVar = TRUE)$ins_status) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("ins_status") %>%
  rename(intercept = `(Intercept)`)

condvar_ins <- attr(lme4::ranef(glmm_ins_office, condVar = TRUE)$ins_status, "postVar")
ranef_ins_df$se <- sqrt(condvar_ins[1, 1, ])

ggplot(ranef_ins_df, aes(x = reorder(ins_status, intercept), y = intercept)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#2C7BB6") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = intercept - 1.96 * se,
                    ymax = intercept + 1.96 * se), width = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Insurance Status Random Effects — Office Visits ",
       subtitle = "Conditional modes ± 1.96 SE",
       x = "", y = "Random Intercept (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r glmm_ins_office_fit, echo=FALSE}
# Compare GLMM vs fixed-effect NB from Part 3
r2_glmm_ins <- MuMIn::r.squaredGLMM(glmm_ins_office)
cat("Marginal R² (fixed effects only):  ", round(r2_glmm_ins[1, "R2m"], 4), "\n")
cat("Conditional R² (fixed + random):   ", round(r2_glmm_ins[1, "R2c"], 4), "\n")
cat("AIC NB fixed-effect model:       ", round(AIC(model_nb_office), 1), "\n")
cat("AIC GLMM (insurance random):     ", round(AIC(glmm_ins_office), 1), "\n")
```

The random-effect variance for insurance status is 0.3306, approximately 9.1% of the residual variability in office visit counts is attributable to systematic differences between insurance categories. The conditional R² rises from 0.170 (fixed effects only) to 0.300 once the random intercept is included, confirming that insurance status carries genuine grouping-level variance beyond what income, age, health status, education, and geography already account for.

The AIC comparison, however, tells a more nuanced story. The GLMM (AIC = 119,843) is worse than the fixed-effect Negative Binomial model from Part 3 (AIC = 119,822). This means that treating insurance status as a random effect — with only three levels — is a less efficient parameterisation than including it as a fixed predictor with explicit, estimable coefficients. 


## GLMM: Insurance Status as Random Effect (ER Visits)
```{r glmm_ins_er, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

theta_er <- model_nb_er$theta

glmm_ins_er <- glmer(
  er_visits ~ region + age_group + sex + race_eth + povcat +
    n_chronic + poor_health + educ_cat + any_barrier +
    (1 | ins_status),
  family = MASS::negative.binomial(theta = theta_er),
  data = meps_adults,
  control = glmerControl(
    optimizer = "bobyqa",
    optCtrl = list(maxfun = 1e5)
  )
)

summary(glmm_ins_er)
```

```{r glmm_ins_er_results, echo=FALSE}
vc_ins_er   <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(glmm_ins_er))
icc_ins_er  <- vc_ins_er$vcov[1] / (vc_ins_er$vcov[1] + (pi^2 / 3))

cat("Random-effect variance (insurance status):", round(vc_ins_er$vcov[1], 4), "\n")
cat("Intraclass Correlation (ICC):", round(icc_ins_er, 4), "\n\n")

glmm_ins_er_tidy <- broom.mixed::tidy(glmm_ins_er, effects = "fixed",
                                       exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  rename(IRR = estimate, CI_low = conf.low, CI_high = conf.high)

knitr::kable(
  glmm_ins_er_tidy %>% dplyr::select(term, IRR, CI_low, CI_high, p.value),
  digits  = 3,
  caption = " Fixed-Effect IRRs ER Visits") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) %>%
  row_spec(which(glmm_ins_er_tidy$p.value < 0.05), bold = TRUE)

r2_glmm_ins_er <- MuMIn::r.squaredGLMM(glmm_ins_er)
cat("Marginal R²:   ", round(r2_glmm_ins_er[1, "R2m"], 4), "\n")
cat("Conditional R²:", round(r2_glmm_ins_er[1, "R2c"], 4), "\n")
cat("AIC NB fixed-effect model:", round(AIC(model_nb_er), 1), "\n")
cat("AIC GLMM (insurance random): ", round(AIC(glmm_ins_er), 1), "\n")
```

For emergency department visits, the random-effect variance for insurance status is 0.0817, yielding an ICC of 0.024 — substantially lower than the office visit ICC (9.1%), consistent with the structural logic from Part 3: insurance status primarily gates entry into the ambulatory circuit, while emergency access is less contingent on coverage type.  
The marginal and conditional R² differ by just 1.2 percentage points (0.058 and 0.070), and the GLMM (AIC = 23,751) is again worse than the fixed-effect NB model (AIC = 23,737) by 14 points. The fixed-effect IRRs replicate Part 3 with full stability.


## GLMM Conclusion
The four GLMMs converge on a consistent conclusion. Region adds negligible explanatory power: geographic disparities are compositional, driven by the concentration of uninsured and low-income individuals.  
Insurance status generates substantially larger clustering, but with only three levels the fixed-effect specification remains more efficient, as both AIC comparisons confirm.  
The structural disparities documented in this analysis are properties of individual circumstances, not of geography or institutional context.

---

# Conclusions
Our analysis confirmed that barriers are real and measurable. 

The Logistic Regression model revealed that being uninsured and belonging to lower income categories are among the strongest predictors of reported access barriers, suggesting that structural inequalities, not just individual health needs, shape whether people receive care.

The Negative Binomial models, chosen to correct for the severe overdispersion present in both office and ER visit counts, further reinforced this picture: uninsured individuals make dramatically fewer office visits, while lower-income groups show higher ER utilization.

The GLMMs added a complementary layer of insight. While insurance status as a random effect introduced modest but non-negligible between-group heterogeneity in office visits (ICC ≈ 9%), its contribution was smaller for ER visits (ICC ≈ 2%), suggesting that for emergency care, individual-level factors, particularly chronic disease burden and poor self-reported health, dominate over insurance clustering. Across all models, the number of chronic conditions and poor health status emerged as the most consistent and powerful drivers of utilization, confirming that unmet clinical need, when not filtered out by financial barriers, translates directly into healthcare demand.
Geographic variation was also present, with the South and West consistently showing lower office visit rates compared to the Northeast, hinting at regional differences in care supply, cultural factors, or underlying health profiles that deserve further investigation.

Taken together, our results paint a consistent picture: in the United States, healthcare access is not purely a function of clinical need. Insurance coverage and income act as gatekeeping mechanisms that redirect, or entirely suppress, utilization.
